how-menu-engineering-works.html.text:
How menu engineering works

Menu engineering sorts every dish on a menu into one of four boxes using two numbers you already have: how many of it sold, and how many dollars it leaves behind after food cost. This page explains where the two thresholds come from, why one of them is weighted, and works a small menu all the way through.

Open the free menu engineering calculator

The two axes

The method is Kasavana and Smith’s, published at Michigan State University in 1982. It has outlasted a lot of fancier ideas because both of its inputs come off a sales report and a recipe card, and neither requires a consultant to interpret.

Popularity is a dish’s share of covers. If every item on a ten-item menu sold equally, each would take 10%. The convention is to call an item popular once it clears 70% of that equal share — so 7% on a ten-item menu, 5.6% on a twelve-item one. The 70% is a convention rather than a law of nature, which is why a calculator worth using prints the threshold it applied instead of asking you to take the sorting on trust.

Contribution margin is menu price minus plate food cost, in dollars. Not as a percentage. This is the axis operators most often get wrong, and the next section is about why.

Why not food cost percentage?

Because food cost percentage and contribution margin disagree constantly, and only one of them pays rent.

DishPricePlate costFood cost %Contributes
Ribeye$34.00$13.6040%$20.40
Pasta$9.00$1.8020%$7.20

The pasta wins by twenty points on the number the industry quotes, and loses by $13.20 on the number that reaches the bank. A kitchen that ranks its menu by food cost percentage will promote the pasta, sell more of it, sell fewer steaks, and end the month with a better food cost percentage and less money. This is the single most common way menu analysis backfires.

Why the margin bar is weighted

The bar every dish is measured against is the menu’s weighted average contribution margin: total contribution margin divided by total covers. Not the average of the per-dish margins.

The difference is not academic. An unweighted average lets a $40 plate that sold twice pull the bar up as hard as the $14 plate that sold four hundred times. The bar is supposed to describe what the menu actually earns per cover, and only the weighted version does that. A menu with one rarely-ordered expensive special can have almost every other dish misclassified by this alone.

The four boxes

  • Star — sells well, contributes above average.
  • Plowhorse — sells well, contributes below average. Volume is doing the work margin should be. Because a plowhorse lands on more plates than anything else, it is where a given price move is worth the most in absolute dollars.
  • Puzzle — contributes above average, does not sell. The margin is already there; what is missing is covers.
  • Dog — below the bar on both. Still takes prep, storage, and a line on the menu.

The names are the industry’s and they are blunter than they need to be. A “dog” can be the dish the owner is proudest of, the one a regular comes in for, or the only vegetarian main on the page. The matrix measures two things and is silent about every other reason a dish earns its place.

A worked menu

Four dishes over four weeks, 1,000 covers. Total sales $16,000, total food cost $5,100, so total contribution margin is $10,900 and the weighted average is $10.90 a cover. Four items, so the equal share is 25% and the popularity bar is 25% × 0.7 = 17.5%.

DishSoldMenu mixPricePlate costCMClass
Smash burger50050.0%$14.00$5.00$9.00Plowhorse
Ribeye10010.0%$34.00$14.00$20.00Puzzle
House salad30030.0%$16.00$3.00$13.00Star
Soup of the day10010.0%$8.00$3.00$5.00Dog

The burger clears the popularity bar easily and contributes $1.90 a plate below the menu average, so it is a plowhorse. The ribeye contributes nearly twice the average and sells at 10%, below the 17.5% bar, so it is a puzzle. Note that the ribeye also has the worst food cost percentage on the menu at 41%, and is the best contributor on it by a wide margin.

What a price move is worth. The burger takes 500 of the 1,000 covers. A $1 increase on it is $500 over these four weeks, about $6,500 a year — if the same number of people order it at the new price. That last clause is the whole risk, and no arithmetic on your own past sales can settle it. Only the next period’s sales report can.

What the matrix does not tell you

It does not tell you what to charge, what to cut, or how to lay out a menu. Those depend on the room, the clientele, what the kitchen can execute on a Saturday, what your suppliers will do to a price next quarter, and a dozen things that are not in four columns of numbers. The matrix gives you a defensible starting point and takes the guesswork out of which dishes are worth arguing about.

Common questions

What is a plowhorse on a menu?

A plowhorse is a dish that sells well but contributes below the menu average in dollars. Volume is doing the work that margin should be. Because a plowhorse lands on more plates than anything else on the menu, a given price move on one is worth more in absolute dollars than the same move anywhere else — which is also why it carries the most risk if the price change moves the mix.

How many dishes do you need for menu engineering to work?

At least two, because both thresholds are relative: an item is measured against the rest of the menu, not against an outside standard. In practice the matrix gets more useful as the menu gets longer, because the popularity bar falls as items are added and the weighted margin bar starts to describe a real mix rather than two or three dishes.

Does menu engineering work for a cafe, food truck or bar?

Yes, wherever you can put a plate cost, a price and a unit count against each item. The method has nothing restaurant-specific in it — it is a portfolio read. For a bar the equivalent per-drink arithmetic, including what an over-pour costs across a year, is a separate calculator on this site.

Should you just remove the dogs from a menu?

That is not a question the matrix answers. It measures two things — covers and contribution margin — and is silent about every other reason a dish earns its place: a regular who comes in for it, the only vegetarian main on the page, an ingredient shared with three other dishes, or the thing that keeps a supplier relationship alive. The matrix tells you which dishes are worth arguing about, not how the argument should end.

Sort your own menu — free, nothing uploaded

No warranty. Verify every figure against your own invoices, POS reports, and accounts, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or repricing a menu with it.       Common questions

      What is menu engineering?

      Menu engineering reads a menu as a portfolio rather than a list of dishes that each succeed or fail on their own. It crosses two axes an operator already has the numbers for — how well an item sells, and how many dollars it contributes after food cost — and sorts every item into one of four quadrants. The method is Kasavana and Smith’s, published at Michigan State in 1982, and it is still the standard because both axes come off a sales report and a recipe card rather than out of a consultant.

      What are stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs?

      A star sells well and contributes above the menu average. A plowhorse sells well and contributes below it — volume is doing the work that margin should be. A puzzle contributes above average but does not sell, so the margin is already there and what is missing is covers. A dog is below the bar on both. The names are the industry’s, not a judgement on the cooking: a dog can be the dish the owner is proudest of.

      Why rank by contribution margin instead of food cost percentage?

      Because the two disagree constantly, and only one of them pays rent. A $34 steak at 40% food cost contributes $20.40 a plate. A $9 pasta at 20% contributes $7.20. The pasta wins on the percentage the industry quotes and loses by $13 on the dollars that actually reach the bank. Ranking a menu by food cost percentage is how a kitchen ends up promoting its cheapest-to-make plate into a worse week.

      How is the popularity threshold calculated?

      If every item on the menu sold equally, each would take an equal share of covers — 10% on a ten-item menu. The convention is to call an item popular once it clears 70% of that equal share, so the bar on a ten-item menu is 7%. It is a convention rather than a law, which is why this calculator prints the threshold it used instead of asking you to take the classification on trust.

      Why is the margin bar weighted by covers?

      Because the bar is meant to represent what the menu actually earns per cover, and an unweighted average does not. Averaging the per-item margins lets a $40 plate that sold twice pull the bar up as hard as the $14 plate that sold four hundred times. This calculator divides total contribution margin by total covers instead, so the bar reflects the mix that actually walked through the door.

      What does the price increase figure assume?

      That the same number of people order the same items at the new price. That assumption is the whole risk in the number, and it is why the figure is printed as arithmetic rather than as a forecast. A price move can change the mix, and nothing in four columns of your own sales data can tell you by how much — only the next period’s sales report can.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Nothing about your dish names, plate costs, menu prices, or cover counts is sent anywhere or stored anywhere but this device. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never any of your numbers.

      Is this accounting, tax, or business advice?

      No. It is arithmetic on the plate costs, menu prices, and unit counts you type in. It has no opinion on what to charge, what to cut, how to lay out a menu, how to treat any of this for tax, or how to run your kitchen — check those against your own records, your POS reports, and a qualified professional before acting on anything here.

vs-averaging-margins-in-a-spreadsheet.ht.text:
← Menu engineering calculator

This calculator vs. averaging margins in a spreadsheet

A menu-engineering spreadsheet built by hand usually bars every dish against =AVERAGE() of the contribution-margin column — one row per dish, not weighted by how many of each actually sold. That single formula choice can flip a menu’s best seller into a dish flagged for a price increase.

What the formula gets wrong

The matrix classifies a dish by comparing its contribution margin — menu price minus plate food cost — against the menu’s own average. The bar is supposed to represent what the menu actually earns per cover. An unweighted =AVERAGE() across the margin column does not measure that: it measures the average dish, counting a special that sold ten times exactly as heavily as a dish that sold three hundred times. A menu is rarely ordered evenly, so that difference is not a rounding error — it can move a dish across the classification line entirely.

This calculator weights the bar by covers instead: total contribution margin across every dish, divided by total units sold. That is the average a plate leaving the kitchen actually clears, not the average a spreadsheet row happens to land on.

A three-dish worked example, four hundred covers total.
DishMarginUnits sold
Chef’s Tasting Plate$30.0010
House Burger$10.00300
Fish Tacos$5.0090

A spreadsheet’s =AVERAGE(30, 10, 5) bar is $15.00. Against that bar the House Burger’s $10.00 margin falls short, and popular plus below-average reads as a plowhorse — a candidate for a price increase. Weighted by covers, the bar is total margin ($3,750) divided by total units (400): $9.38. Against that bar the same $10.00 burger clears it, and popular plus above-average reads as a star — the dish carrying three quarters of every cover the menu served, correctly read as the one already earning its keep. The ten-cover special is what pulled the unweighted average above the burger’s own margin in the first place; it barely moves the weighted one.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Open the free menu engineering calculator

Common questions

What does a spreadsheet menu-engineering worksheet usually get wrong?

Its “menu average” bar is usually built as =AVERAGE() across the contribution-margin column — one row per dish, unweighted. That treats a dish sold ten times over the period the same as a dish sold three hundred times: each row counts once in the average regardless of how many actually went out the door. The bar is supposed to represent what the menu earns per cover, and an unweighted mean of the rows does not measure that — it measures the average dish, not the average plate served.

Can you show a real example of the misclassification?

A three-dish menu: a Chef's Tasting Plate at $30.00 margin, ten sold; a House Burger at $10.00 margin, three hundred sold; and Fish Tacos at $5.00 margin, ninety sold — four hundred covers total. A spreadsheet's =AVERAGE(30, 10, 5) bar is $15.00, so the $10.00 House Burger falls below it and reads as a plowhorse needing a price move. Weighted by covers — total margin divided by total covers, $3,750 over 400 — the bar is $9.38, so that same $10.00 burger, three quarters of every plate that left the kitchen, clears the bar and is a star. The ten-cover special is what pulled the unweighted average above the burger's margin in the first place.

Why does an unweighted average distort the bar so much?

Because a menu is rarely evenly ordered, and the distortion gets worse the more lopsided the covers are. A low-volume special with a high per-plate margin pulls an unweighted average up without contributing much to the menu's actual dollars, while the dish carrying most of the covers is judged against a number its own sales never produced. Weighting by covers — total contribution margin divided by total units sold — fixes that by construction: it is the bar the menu's real mix actually clears, not the bar a row-by-row average happens to land on.

Does this replace building a menu-engineering spreadsheet entirely?

For getting the weighted bar and the classification right, yes — that is the one job this calculator does, for free, with nothing uploaded. It keeps no history across periods and no year-over-year trend the way a spreadsheet an operator maintains themselves can. An operator who wants to track how a dish's classification moves month to month still has reasons to keep a sheet alongside it — as long as its average is weighted by covers, not by rows.

Nothing here says or implies that keeping a menu-engineering spreadsheet is a mistake — it is how most independent operators already do this, and the arithmetic only breaks down at the one formula choice described above. The Chef’s Tasting Plate / House Burger / Fish Tacos example is a worked illustration built for this page, not a claim about any specific restaurant’s real menu.

This calculator vs. MarginEdge

Two different jobs. MarginEdge is an account-based back-office platform that keeps a restaurant’s plate costs current by reading its supplier invoices. This page is a free, private worksheet for the read those costs are for — which dishes are carrying the menu, which are being carried, and what one price move across the plowhorses is worth over a year.

What each tool is for

MarginEdge is a restaurant back-office platform. Its central mechanism is invoice processing: you send in supplier invoices and they come back digitised line by line, so plate costs and food cost percentage move on their own as ingredient prices move. Around that it offers inventory counting, ordering, recipe and plate costing, and integrations out to point-of-sale systems and accounting software. It is an ongoing paid subscription, used through an account, and it is where a restaurant’s cost data actually lives. No plan name, price or feature list for MarginEdge is quoted anywhere on this page: the vendor’s own material is not reachable from the session that generated it, and only the well-documented category facts above are stated.

This calculator does none of that. It reads no invoices, connects to no POS, stores nothing and has no account. You give it three numbers per dish — plate food cost, menu price, and units sold over a period — and it returns the Kasavana and Smith classification for every dish, the two thresholds it used, the menu’s overall food cost percentage against a target you set, and the size of one stated price increase applied across the plowhorses, over the period and annualised. It runs free in any browser and uploads nothing you type.

I need inventory counts, purchase ordering, and my books to reconcile.MarginEdge, or a comparable platform — this calculator touches none of it.

They answer different questions, and a restaurant that runs on MarginEdge still has to make the call this calculator is for. MarginEdge is a restaurant back-office platform: you send it your supplier invoices, it digitises them line by line, and it keeps plate costs and food cost moving as prices change, with inventory counts, ordering, and links out to your POS and your accounting software. It is an account-based paid subscription and it is where a restaurant's cost data lives. This calculator holds no data at all. You type in each dish's plate food cost, its menu price and how many sold over a period, and it classifies every dish against the menu's own weighted-average contribution margin and a popularity bar set at 70% of an equal share, then prints both thresholds so you can disagree with them. A restaurant that wants plate costs to stay accurate on their own, without anyone retyping an invoice, is better served by MarginEdge or a comparable back-office platform. An operator who wants to see this menu sorted into stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs right now, for free, without an account, and with the arithmetic shown rather than asserted, is in the right place here.

vs-ranking-by-food-cost-percent.html.text:
← Menu Engineering Calculator

This calculator vs. ranking by food cost percentage

Food cost percentage is the number restaurants already track on every dish. This page is about what changes when a menu gets sorted by contribution margin and popularity instead — the matrix this calculator runs.

What each approach is

Ranking by food cost percentage means reading down a menu or a POS report and judging each dish by ingredient cost divided by menu price — the number most kitchens already track, dish by dish, without a separate tool. It costs nothing and needs no extra data, and it is the default nearly every operator starts from, because it is the number suppliers, POS systems and recipe cards already report.

This calculator takes the same three numbers a food-cost read already needs — plate food cost, menu price and units sold over a period — and crosses two different axes: contribution margin in dollars against the menu's own weighted-average, and popularity against a 70% share-of-equal-sales bar. It runs once, in the browser, on nothing that leaves the device, and it sorts every dish into a star, plowhorse, puzzle or dog instead of a single percentage.

The gap is not rounding error. On this calculator's own shipped four-dish example, ranking by food cost percentage puts a $34.00 ribeye last on the menu at 41.2% — the worst dish by that measure. The matrix classifies the same ribeye as a puzzle: at $20.00 a plate, its contribution margin is nearly double the menu's $10.90 weighted average. It is not overpriced on ingredients; it simply is not selling enough, at 10% of covers against a 17.5% popularity bar. The percentage ranking also has nothing to say about the smash burger, which sits mid-table at 35.7% food cost but is the plowhorse doing half the menu's volume at a below-average margin — the one dish where a price move pays off on the most plates. A $1.00 increase there alone is worth $500 over the four weeks entered, or about $6,500 a year, a number the percentage ranking never surfaces because nothing about that dish's own percentage stands out.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Which dish has the lowest food cost percentage?The ranking — free, and already what most kitchens track dish by dish.
Which dishes are actually carrying this menu in dollars, and which are being carried?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account, no upload.
Is the dish with the worst food cost percentage actually the problem?Run the same menu through this calculator and compare the two readings directly.
Which dish is a price increase actually worth acting on?This calculator's plowhorse figure — on the shipped example, not the dish with the worst percentage.
How does the math behind the matrix actually work?This calculator's own worked explanation.
Do I need to create an account, upload sales data, or sign up?No, for either approach — the percentage ranking needs nothing and neither does this calculator.

Food cost percentage is not a bad number so much as an incomplete one: useful for pricing a single dish, misleading when it is asked to rank a whole menu against itself. This calculator does not throw the percentage away — it still reports it, per dish and overall — it just stops treating it as the only column a dish gets judged by.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Why not just rank the menu by food cost percentage?

Because food cost percentage and contribution margin rank a menu in a different order, and only contribution margin is the dollar amount that pays rent. On this calculator's own shipped four-dish example, a ribeye priced at $34.00 against a $14.00 plate cost runs 41.2% food cost; a house salad priced at $16.00 against a $3.00 plate cost runs 18.8%. Ranked by the lower percentage, the salad looks like the better dish and the ribeye looks like the worst one on the menu. Ranked by contribution margin, the ribeye contributes $20.00 a plate and the salad contributes $13.00 -- the ribeye is the higher-margin item, and food cost percentage ranked it backwards.

How much does it actually change on a real menu?

On the calculator's shipped four-dish example, ranking by food cost percentage alone (lowest to highest) puts the house salad first at 18.8%, the smash burger second at 35.7%, the soup of the day third at 37.5%, and the ribeye last at 41.2% -- worst on the menu by that measure. This calculator's matrix classifies the ribeye as a puzzle instead: at $20.00 a plate its contribution margin is nearly double the menu's $10.90 weighted-average, and the only thing working against it is that it sells at 10% of covers against a 17.5% popularity bar -- it does not need a lower food cost, it needs more covers. The percentage ranking also buries the one dish the matrix flags as worth acting on: the smash burger sits mid-table on food cost percentage (35.7%) but is the plowhorse, 50% of covers at a below-average $9.00 margin, the only item on this menu where a price move lands on enough plates to matter. A $1.00 increase on the smash burger alone is worth $500 over the four weeks entered, or about $6,500 a year -- a number the percentage ranking never surfaces, because nothing about the burger's own percentage stands out from the rest of the menu.

Doesn't a low food cost percentage still matter?

Yes -- it is one of the numbers a kitchen should watch, just not the only one a dish should be judged by. On its own it answers how much of one plate's own price is food cost, not how many dollars the dish contributed or whether enough people ordered it. This calculator still reports every dish's food cost percentage, plus the menu's overall food cost percentage against a target you set -- it is one column on the results table, not a number this tool throws away. What changes is that it stops being the only column a dish gets judged by.

What does the price-increase figure actually show?

It sizes one specific move: raising price by a stated amount on every dish the matrix classifies as a plowhorse (sells well, contributes below the menu's weighted-average margin), assuming the same number of people order it at the new price. On the shipped four-dish example the only plowhorse is the smash burger, and a $1.00 increase across its 500 units sold over the four weeks entered is worth $500 in that period, or about $6,500 annualized. Food cost percentage ranking has no equivalent figure, because it never singles out which dish a price move would pay off on the most covers.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests for either approach. Ranking by food cost percentage is arithmetic you can already do on a spreadsheet or by hand from your own sales report. This calculator's matrix runs the same way -- entirely in your browser, on this device, with nothing about your dish names, plate costs, menu prices or cover counts sent or stored anywhere else.

Is this accounting or business advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the plate costs, menu prices and units sold you type in. It has no opinion on what to charge, what to cut or how to lay out a menu -- check its output against your own records, your POS reports, and a qualified professional before acting on anything here.
